question.problem:
Find the solution to the inequality $\frac{y+2}{3}<\frac{y+3}{2}.$

The solution is $y$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
First, we clear the rational expressions by multiplying both sides of the inequality by the lowest common positive multiple of the denominators:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+2}{3} & <\frac{y+3}{2} \\ 6\cdot (\frac{y+2}{3}) & <6\cdot (\frac{y+3}{2}) \\ 2\cdot (y+2) & <3\cdot (y+3) \\ 2y+4 & <3y+9\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles. 

Remember, when we divide an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y+4 & <3y+9 \\ 2y+4-3y & <3y+9-3y \\ 4-y & <9 \\ 4-y-4 & <9-4 \\ -y & <5 \\ \frac{-y}{-1} & \,\,>\,\,\frac{5}{-1} \\ y & >-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y>-5.$
